ety.text: Inherited from Middle English sippen, of uncertain origin. Compare with Low German sippen (“to sip”). Possibly from a variant of Middle English suppen (“to drink, sip”) (see sup) or perhaps from Old English sipian, sypian (“to take in moisture, soak, macerate”), from Proto-Germanic *sipōną (“to drip, trickle”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, trickle, leak out”). Compare also Old High German supfen (“to drink, sip”), from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną (“to sip, intake”).

ex: So order one more coffee / Have another sip of wine / We can go on talking / Until it's disco closing time

senses.d: An event at which people drink alcohol in small, usually subintoxicating amounts.
ex: Earl is always a good time. His appearance at parties, whether it's a smart cocktail sip or a basement gig, is mandatory.

senses.d: To drink slowly, small mouthfuls at a time.
ex: A waiter brought his aperitif, which was a small scotch and soda, and as he sipped it gratefully he sighed.
bright young things in jeans and T-shirts huddle around laptops, sipping lattes or munching on free food.
[She] rais'd it to her mouth with sober grace; / Then, sipping, offered to the next in place.

senses.d: To taste the liquor of; to drink out of.
ex: They skim the floods, and sip the purple flowers.
Even when turned off, these devices can idly sip electricity from your outlet costing you money.
It makes a small car, the Chevy Cobalt, which sips petrol in moderation and is therefore selling well.

ety.text: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin sorsum, *sorpsum, from sorptum, from alteration of Latin sorbitum, supine of sorbeō (“to suck”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorbīre, from Latin sorbēre.
Inherited from Old Spanish sorber, inherited from Latin sorbēre. Spanish forms showing the expected stem-vowel diphthongization do occur regionally.
